lead: An optical network is a set of nodes joined by fiber links. A connection that stays in the optical domain from one end to the other is a lightpath, and it holds one wavelength on every link it crosses. Networks exist because one fiber between two points is not enough: many users, many cities and many services must share the same fiber plant. Telephone companies use these ideas in access, metro and core networks; the same vocabulary describes a campus fiber ring or a data-centre link.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the wavelength grid and Unit 5 for span loss and power budget.

blocks.text: A node is a point where traffic is added, dropped, switched or regenerated. A link is the fiber between adjacent nodes. A span is one amplified section inside a link; its loss must fit the power budget (Unit 5). A path is the ordered set of nodes and links between a source and a destination. A channel is one wavelength on one link. A wavelength is the optical carrier taken from the grid in 6.1.

A lightpath is an end-to-end connection that uses one wavelength on every link of its path and does not convert to electronics in between. Some syllabi call it a wavelength path or an optical channel. The physical topology is the actual graph of nodes and links. The logical or lightpath topology is the graph of lightpaths seen by the routers. A mesh of fibers can present a ring of lightpaths, and a ring of fibers can present a full mesh.

A transparent network keeps the signal optical end to end. Impairments add up (Unit 2), so reach is limited. An opaque network regenerates at nodes: it receives, reamplifies, reshapes and retimes, then retransmits (3R). Regeneration restores the signal but costs a transponder at each side. A static lightpath is set up once and left; a switched lightpath is set up on demand.

Common physical topologies are mesh, ring, star and bus. Mesh has many links and survives cuts, but needs more ports. Ring is a closed loop; two fibers often form a self-healing ring. Star has one central node; bus shares one fiber. The public telecommunication network is built in three tiers. The access network joins homes, offices and mobile towers to the first exchange. Its reach is a few kilometres up to about 20 km; a passive optical network splits one fiber among many users. The metro network joins exchanges inside a city, typically tens of kilometres. It is usually a ring because a city has rights-of-way along roads and a ring gives a simple backup path. The core or long-haul network joins cities and countries, typically hundreds to thousands of kilometres. It is a mesh of cross-connects and amplifiers; a Delhi–Mumbai route is a core link.

The tier sets what matters: access fights cost per user, metro fights fast protection, core fights capacity and reach. The logical topology can be richer than the physical one. Six metro nodes on one ring can still have 15 lightpaths, one per pair, as the example shows.

An optical node performs four jobs. Add/drop puts local wavelengths into or out of the fiber (OADM). Cross-connect moves a wavelength from an input fiber to a chosen output fiber (OXC). Regeneration recreates a clean signal when the path is too long. Switching sets or changes the route under control. Simple nodes do only add/drop; larger nodes do all four. The node hardware is in 6.7.

Protection reserves capacity before a failure. In 1+1 the signal is sent on two paths at once and the receiver selects the better; no extra traffic rides the backup. In 1:1 one backup path serves one working path and may carry low-priority extra traffic when healthy. In 1:N one backup serves N working paths. Restoration finds a new route after the failure, so it is slower and needs a control plane. Rings dominate metro because a fiber cut becomes a loop-back at the two nodes next to the cut, and protection can finish in milliseconds.

A broadcast-and-select network sends all wavelengths to all nodes; each receiver filters the one it wants. A wavelength-routed network sends each wavelength through cross-connects along its own path. Static lightpaths are fixed; switched lightpaths are set up and torn down by signalling. The wavelength must be the same on every link unless the node has a wavelength converter.

examples.question: A metro ring has 6 nodes. Each node must send one 10 Gb/s lightpath to each of the other five. (a) How many node pairs are there? (b) How many wavelengths are needed if one wavelength per pair carries both directions and there is no wavelength reuse? (c) How many with 1+1 protection? (d) What is the total carried working traffic?
steps: Label the number of nodes N = 6. Count each pair once because the lightpath is bidirectional: pairs = N(N − 1) ÷ 2 = 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 pairs.
With no wavelength reuse, each pair needs its own wavelength on every link: 15 wavelengths.
1+1 protection sends a copy on a second wavelength for each pair: 2 × 15 = 30 wavelengths. The transponder count also doubles.
Each pair carries 10 Gb/s of working traffic: total working traffic = 15 × 10 Gb/s = 150 Gb/s. The protection copy repeats the same data, so it is not extra working traffic.
examples.answer: The ring has 15 pairs, 15 working wavelengths, 30 wavelengths with 1+1 protection, and 150 Gb/s of working traffic.
examples.check:
N = 6
rate = 10
pairs = N * (N - 1) // 2
wavelengths = pairs
protected = 2 * wavelengths
traffic = pairs * rate
print(pairs)
print(wavelengths)
print(protected)
print(traffic)

traps: Physical topology is not the lightpath topology. A ring of fiber can carry a mesh of lightpaths, so do not copy the fiber graph into the logical graph.
Protection doubles both wavelengths and transponders. Count the second copy on every link of the protected path, not just on one link.
A lightpath needs the same wavelength on every link unless a converter is present. A free wavelength on one link is not enough.
1+1 and 1:1 look like backups, but 1+1 is always bridged and its backup carries no extra traffic; a 1:1 backup can carry extra traffic when healthy.
Link, span, path and channel are not synonyms. A channel is one wavelength on one link; a lightpath is end to end.

quiz.q: Define a lightpath and a channel.
quiz.a: A lightpath is an end-to-end optical connection that uses one wavelength on every link of its path. A channel is one wavelength on one link.

quiz.q: Why can the logical topology differ from the physical topology?
quiz.a: The physical topology is the graph of fibers and nodes. The logical topology is the graph of lightpaths set up over those fibers. One fiber mesh can carry a ring of lightpaths, or one fiber ring can carry a full mesh of lightpaths.

quiz.q: A 5-node ring gives one 10 Gb/s lightpath to each pair, with no wavelength reuse and 1+1 protection. Find (a) the number of pairs, (b) the number of wavelengths, (c) the working traffic.
quiz.a: (a) 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 pairs. (b) 10 working wavelengths; 1+1 doubles this to 20 wavelengths. (c) 10 × 10 Gb/s = 100 Gb/s of working traffic.

quiz.q: Why do metro networks use rings more than meshes?
quiz.a: A metro has fibers along roads and rights-of-way, which naturally form a ring. A ring gives two disjoint directions between nodes, so a single cut can be looped back at the two nodes next to the cut. Protection is simple and fast, and fewer ports are needed than in a mesh.

quiz.q: Contrast a transparent network with an opaque network.
quiz.a: A transparent network keeps the signal optical end to end, so impairments accumulate and reach is limited. An opaque network regenerates at nodes with 3R, which restores the signal but costs a transponder at each side.

In 1+1 the signal is bridged on two paths all the time and the receiver selects one; the backup carries no extra traffic. In 1:1 one backup path is reserved for one working path and may carry low-priority extra traffic when the working path is healthy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real metro and core networks now use reconfigurable optical add/drop multiplexers and colourless, directionless cross-connects, so a lightpath can be changed without touching fiber. Control planes and software-defined networking set up switched lightpaths automatically. Elastic optical networks pack channels with different widths instead of a fixed grid. Search next for ROADM, flexible grid, and optical network control plane.
